security_spec.violation_condition: On RV32 QEMU (TARGET_LONG_BITS=32), pmp_update_rule_addr() at pmp.c:256-257 computes sa = prev_addr << 2 and ea = (this_addr << 2) - 1u, where prev_addr/this_addr are 32-bit target_ulong but sa/ea are 64-bit hwaddr. The << 2 is evaluated in 32-bit arithmetic before assignment. For pmpaddr values representing physical addresses above 4 GiB (pmpaddr >= 0x40000000, i.e. pa[33:32] != 00), the shift overflows 32 bits, truncating the high address bits. The PMP range aliases into low 4 GiB space or becomes empty (sa > ea), violating the spec requirement that TOR PMP correctly addresses up to 2^XLEN+2.
security_spec.summary: RV32 TOR PMP << 2 overflow truncates physical addresses >= 4 GiB, aliasing PMP protections into low memory and defeating access control

findings.finding: Integer overflow in TOR PMP address computation: prev_addr and this_addr are target_ulong (uint32_t on RV32), but the << 2 shift is evaluated in 32-bit arithmetic before assignment to 64-bit hwaddr sa/ea. For pmpaddr values representing physical addresses above 4 GiB (pmpaddr >= 0x40000000, i.e. pa[33:32] != 00), the shift overflows 32 bits, truncating the high bits. The PMP range aliases into low 4 GiB space, violating the spec requirement (machine.adoc:3390-3392) that RV32 PMP must support 34-bit physical addresses. This allows attacker-controlled M-mode code to bypass PMP protections on high physical memory.
findings.snippet:
sa = prev_addr << 2; /* shift up from [xx:0] to [xx+2:2] */
        ea = (this_addr << 2) - 1u;

spec_citations.excerpt: The Sv32 page-based virtual-memory scheme described in <<sv32>> supports 34-bit physical addresses for RV32, so the PMP scheme must support addresses wider than XLEN for RV32. The Sv39 and Sv48 page-based virtual-memory schemes described in <<sv39>> and <<sv48>> support a 56-bit physical address space, so the RV64 PMP address registers impose the same limit.

It is not possible to represent the address 2^XLEN+2 as the top of a range, so, for example, in an RV32 system with 34-bit physical addresses, a TOR PMP cannot be used to give less-privileged modes access to the uppermost word of memory. Either a NAPOT PMP can be used, or that memory can be left inaccessible to less-privileged modes.
draw-box "address[33:2]" — RV32 pmpaddr register encodes physical address bits [33:2], confirming 34-bit physical address support.

findings.finding: Same integer overflow in NA4 PMP address computation: this_addr is target_ulong (uint32_t on RV32), so this_addr << 2 is evaluated in 32-bit arithmetic. For pmpaddr >= 0x40000000 on RV32, the NA4 region aliases into low 4 GiB space. Unlike TOR (which also has a prev_addr shift), NA4 only has one shift, but the same overflow applies.
findings.snippet:
sa = this_addr << 2; /* shift up from [xx:0] to [xx+2:2] */
        ea = (sa + 4u) - 1u;

spec_citations.excerpt: The Sv32 page-based virtual-memory scheme described in <<sv32>> supports 34-bit physical addresses for RV32, so the PMP scheme must support addresses wider than XLEN for RV32.

findings.finding: NAPOT path is safe: pmp_decode_napot receives this_addr as hwaddr (uint64_t) due to implicit integer promotion of target_ulong to hwaddr at the call site (line 266). The shift a = (a << 2) | 0x3 operates on 64-bit hwaddr, correctly handling physical addresses above 4 GiB on RV32.

pmpaddr_csr_read() returns pmpaddr values as target_ulong (32-bit on RV32), matching the 32-bit CSR register width. This is architecturally correct (the CSR is 32 bits wide on RV32) and the read-masking logic for OFF/TOR/NAPOT modes is correct. However, the write path at line 603 stores the raw target_ulong value without range validation. While the spec defines pmpaddr as WARL, QEMU does not enforce the WARL constraint that high bits beyond the physical address width should be read-only zero. This is not a security bug per se (the pmpaddr register is architecturally 32-bit), but means guest software could observe inconsistent behavior if it writes values with upper bits set and expects them to be masked.

spec_citations.excerpt: PMP address register format, RV32 — the register holds address[33:2] in 32 bits, so no WARL masking beyond G bits is needed; the CSR width itself is the limit.

findings.finding: The G-bit masking for TOR correctly uses 1ULL (64-bit unsigned long long) on both prev_addr and this_addr, ensuring the bitmask is 64-bit and properly clearing low G bits before comparison. This masking is safe regardless of XLEN.

spec_citations.excerpt: When G >= 1 and pmpcfg_i.A[1] is clear, i.e. the mode is OFF or TOR, then bits pmpaddr_i[G-1:0] read as all zeros. Bits pmpaddr_i[G-1:0] do not affect the TOR address-matching logic.
